1. Um … zu or damit?
Both express purpose (in order to / so that). The rule for choosing is simple:
um … zu + infinitive
Er zieht um, um näher bei Mara zu wohnen. (he – he)
damit + clause (verb at the end)
Wir helfen ihm, damit er schneller fertig ist. (we – him)
I'm learning German in order to work in Berlin. (I – I)
I'm explaining slowly so that you understand. (I – you)
“damit” can also be used with the same subject: “Ich stehe früh auf, damit ich pünktlich bin.” But “um … zu” is more elegant.
After “damit” you don't use the modals “wollen” or “sollen” (the purpose is already included): “…, damit er kommt”, not “damit er kommen soll”. But “können” is common: “…, damit du kommen kannst.”
2. Sodass: consequence
“sodass” (or “so dass”) shows the result: “so, so that”. The verb goes to the END:
He missed the train, so he was late.
3. So … dass: so… that
When you want to emphasise a quality, you put “so” before the adjective and “dass” at the start of the subordinate clause:
The cushions are so light that Bruno could carry them.
She was so tired that she fell asleep immediately.
With nouns: “so viel(e) …, dass” / “so ein(e) …, dass”: “Es gab so viele Kartons, dass der Flur voll war.”

Ein neuer Nachbar

The move started at eight in the morning, and at half past eight it started to rain, so all the boxes that were already on the pavement had to be carried into the hallway of the house. The removal van was too big for narrow Kastanienallee, so it had to park two houses further down. And the driver had forgotten to bring the blankets used to protect the furniture. It was, as Ludwig put it, a perfectly normal Berlin move.

But the house helped. Piotr carried boxes, two at a time, until his back protested. Andrei assembled the bed, with a drill he had borrowed from Ludwig and which was so loud that Bruno hid under Kuba's bed. Lena brought coffee and a huge plum cake, so that nobody would give up from hunger. Kasia cleaned the windows, so that Jakob could watch the sunset over the rooftops on his first evening.

Kuba was everywhere at once. He carried cushions, lamps, pots, a cactus and in the end even a small box of books, so proud that he went up and down the stairs three times, just to show he could. The fact that his teacher now lived next door, wall to wall, seemed to him both wonderful and a little unsettling. “Can you hear when I'm not doing my homework?” he asked. “Only if you make so much noise that the whole house hears it,” said Jakob.

Jakob carried the cello himself. He took it up the stairs in its big black case, slowly, step by step, the way you carry a child. It was his grandmother's cello, more than a hundred years old, and it had already survived three moves: from a village in Thuringia to Weimar, from Weimar to Berlin on Oderberger Straße, and now to Kastanienallee. When he got to the top, he opened the case and checked every string before sitting down. Only then did he drink his coffee.

At twelve o'clock they all took a break in the courtyard, under the chestnut tree, which in August was so dense that not a single raindrop came through the leaves. Lena had put the plum cake on the old wooden table, and Andrei was handing out coffee in mugs he had brought from the bakery. While they were eating, Andrei told them that he had finished the first semester of his master's with the top mark and that his professor had offered him a job as an assistant. “So that I don't live only on pretzels,” he said. Lena elbowed him in the ribs. “You don't live on pretzels,” she said. “You live on me.” They all laughed. Then Lena said, a little more quietly, that she was thinking of expanding the bakery. The shop next door, an old shoe shop, would become free in the autumn. “I want to open a small café next door,” she said. “With three tables. So that people don't just buy bread, but stay too.” Ludwig, who had just come into the courtyard, heard this and said nothing. But Mara saw him smile, so proud that he suddenly looked ten years younger.

In the afternoon, when most of the boxes had been unpacked and everyone was sitting exhausted on the floor, there was a knock at the door. It was Ludwig, with Fritz, with a sheet of paper and a pen. He was wearing his white shirt, as if for an official appointment.
Mr Lorenz. The tenancy agreement. Please sign here. And here. And here, this is the most important one.

Jakob read the last page. On it, in Ludwig's large, shaky handwriting, below the usual paragraphs about rent, deposit and house rules, there was an extra point: “§ 12. The tenant undertakes to make music at the next courtyard party, so that the tradition of the house continues. In addition, he undertakes to take very good care of the tenant on the third floor, so good that the landlord doesn't have to worry.”

Jakob laughed and signed. Mara blushed. Ludwig took the agreement, folded it neatly and put it in his shirt pocket. Then he gave Jakob a key, an old, heavy brass key. “For the front door,” he said. “And for the cellar. So that you never have to carry your cello anywhere again.”

In the evening, after everyone had left, Jakob and Mara sat on the floor in the new flat, among the last boxes. The yellow walls glowed in the light of the setting sun, so warm that the flat already looked like a home. Jakob picked up his cello and played, for the first time in this house, a slow piece by Bach. It sounded so full and so deep that Mara felt the old wooden floor vibrating beneath her.

And then, after a few minutes, they heard it. From above, from the fourth floor, through the open windows, a piano answered. Mrs Hoffmann had come back from Lübeck a week earlier. She played the same melody, two bars later, like an echo, and then together with the cello, as if the two of them had been rehearsing for years. On the first floor a window opened. On the second floor, next door, Kuba pressed his nose against the glass. Down in the courtyard, Fritz lay down under the chestnut tree and listened.

When the piece was over, Mrs Hoffmann called down from the window: “Mr Lorenz! You're playing the adagio too fast. Tomorrow at three at my place. So that we can practise it.” Jakob laughed and called back that he would be punctual. Mara rested her head on his shoulder. She thought that in this house nobody stayed alone. Not even a cello.

Later, when Mara wanted to go up to her own flat on the third floor, she stopped on the stairs. One floor below her now lived Jakob. One floor above her, Mrs Hoffmann. Two floors down, Ludwig, and right at the bottom Lena and Andrei, in the bakery. She thought of her first night in this house, almost four years ago, when she hadn't known anyone and had been so lonely that she had stood at the window until it got light. Now the house was so full of people she loved that sometimes she didn't know which door to knock on first. She went up, opened her window and looked down into the courtyard. Fritz was still lying under the chestnut tree. He looked up at her and wagged his tail once, as if he wanted to say: I know. I've been here from the start.

She didn't close the window. It was a warm August night, and from the second floor she could hear soft music. Jakob was still practising the adagio, more slowly this time, the way Mrs Hoffmann wanted. Mara lay down and listened until she fell asleep. It was the first night she fell asleep to music from two directions: the piano from above, the cello from below. Like a house that sings.

Tipps für den Umzug
Start packing early, so that there's no stress on the last day.
Write on every box what's in it and which room it goes in. That way you'll find everything quickly.
Put books in small boxes. Big boxes of books are so heavy that nobody can carry them.
Ask your friends for help to save money. But don't forget to order pizza and drinks.
And introduce yourself to the neighbours on the first day, so that you settle in quickly.
